The playground demos follow a fixed instrument grammar, settled 2026-08-19 on
exhibit two (the rebake demo) after several rounds with Eric:

- **Chrome header:** state gauge top-left (`live` cyan / `working` amber — the
  panel's ONE in-flight signal); view controls top-right (e.g. the SLOW MOTION
  switch — "the corner every editor keeps its view switches"). No panel label:
  the intro prose names the subject once.
- **Body:** the specimen (big value + provenance rows as one aligned table) +
  one narration caption. Feedback trilogy: gauge flips, display dims/pulses
  while a round trip is out, one amber landing wash on value change
  (`.ht-land`, key-remount, skips first mount, reduced-motion safe).
- **Deck:** actions only, execution order, bottom strip.
- **Reference bar:** bottom chrome — code drawer (`▸ file.ts`, shiki source
  opens inside the chassis) left, `↗ docs ↗ source` pinned right (absolute,
  so clicks don't toggle). No readout strip: the source IS the spec plate.
- Asides render as `/* … */` code comments in comment-gray mono (MetaAside
  `variant="comment"`); exhibit order rides in the eyebrow (`02 · topic`),
  the watermark chapter numeral is retired as course furniture.

**Principles behind it:** engineer-not-student; one experience legible to all
four audiences (no persona modes — use redundant encoding instead: the
BakeSwatch renders `#` + first 6 hash chars as the color the hash spells,
unlabeled, discovery intended); every element re-argued against clarity;
client-owned state paints on the click frame, only server sync lives in
transitions.

**Migration state (2026-08-19):** exhibit 02 fully migrated. Exhibits 01, 03,
04, 05 still on legacy shape (LivePanel `label`/`readout` props, standalone
CodeBlocks, old links row) — migration is mostly mechanical via `ReferenceBar`
+ `CodeBlock variant="bar"`. Eyebrow + comment asides already applied
globally through the shared DemoSection.

**Banked ideas:** fruit/emoji hash encoding as a possible easter-egg layer
(rejected as primary — breaks instrument discipline); swatches in the
machinery comparison rows (blocked: details are strings with width-reservation
tests — needs a proper JSX StableSlot design); digest beats: the
side-effect-runs-twice warning, and the swatch-is-the-hash reveal.

Verification rule: `next dev` lies about cache semantics — preview deploys
are the truth-bench (see [[project-env-quirks]]).

---
name: project-env-quirks
description: "Machine/env quirks on Eric's Mac that bite headless agent sessions (docker pulls, biome gate)"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: b10586c9-1b13-412f-92b7-ddd260a6528c
  modified: 2026-08-19T13:25:22.586Z
---

Two environment quirks hit during the knowledge-hub build (2026-07-11):

1. **`docker pull` hangs forever in headless sessions.** `~/.docker/config.json` has `credsStore: "desktop"` plus a Docker Scout hook on `pull`; the credential helper blocks on macOS Keychain without a UI. Even `docker run` hangs at "Unable to find image locally".
   **How to apply:** `mkdir -p /tmp/docker-nocreds && echo '{}' > /tmp/docker-nocreds/config.json`, then `DOCKER_CONFIG=/tmp/docker-nocreds docker pull …` — completes in seconds. `docker ps`/`exec`/`run` (with image present) work normally.

2. **Biome gate (ultracite v7 extends paths): fixed per-branch, not repo-wide.** biome.jsonc must extend `ultracite/biome/*` (v7 layout), not the v5-era `ultracite/core|react|next`; check/fix scripts must run the local ultracite pin, never `@latest`. Applied on Kheirah/agent-knowledge-hub-design (484e1a0 + 26327a7, 2026-07-11) and independently re-derived on Kheirah/continue-prev-task (fe73b90, 2026-07-12) — branches cut before those commits will still show "Could not resolve ultracite/core"; apply the same two-line fix. Repo-wide pre-existing findings remain (hundreds; scoped `bunx biome check <path>` is the usable gate for new work). The masterclass exhibit dir is mechanically clean as of fe73b90 (~36 judgment-rule findings left: noJsxPropsBind, noExportedImports, index keys).
   **Zombie dirty files:** entire.io (manual-commit strategy) snapshots uncommitted changes to a shadow branch and re-applies them post-commit ("carried forward remaining files") — a plain `git checkout --` of unwanted noise gets silently undone at the next commit. Cure: `git checkout -- <files> && entire clean --force` (drops the HEAD shadow branch + session carry-forward state; committed checkpoint history is unaffected).
   Also: Biome's `useSortedKeys` assist auto-sorts object keys on `--write` — it silently reorders semantically-ordered literals (MongoDB compound-index key specs). Guard such files with `// biome-ignore-all assist/source/useSortedKeys: …`.

3. **Vercel:** hasToggle.dev deploys as project `has-toggle-dev-web` under team scope `spiritsdontfly` (not the default `kheirahs-projects`, not `forsuxess`). Use `vercel ls/inspect --scope spiritsdontfly`; `vercel inspect --logs <url>` pulls build logs without switching scope. (2026-07-24)

4. **Bun override staleness:** after adding a root `overrides` entry, plain `bun install` updates `bun.lock` but can leave stale `.bun` store symlinks (nested dep still resolving to the old version). `rm -rf node_modules && bun install` is required for the override to actually take effect. (2026-07-24, radix-slot pin)

5. **The `web` app's locale-prefixed URLs 500 in dev.** `http://localhost:3001/en/learn/...` dies in middleware (`[NEMO] Middleware execution failed`); the unprefixed `http://localhost:3001/learn/...` serves fine. Use the unprefixed path when driving the site in a browser or the masterclass page looks broken when it isn't. `curl` also 500s on both (the middleware chain needs real browser headers) — verify with Playwright/Chrome DevTools, not curl. Next 16 also refuses to start a second dev server for the same project dir ("Run kill <pid> to stop it"), so reuse Eric's running server on 3001 rather than starting your own. (2026-07-25)

6. **Shared `.next` dir: `next build` then `next dev` corrupts some routes.** Running dev after a prod build in the same `apps/web/.next` produces `SyntaxError: Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON` and 500s on a subset of routes (hit the nuqs-using learn pages, 2026-07-31, Next 16.2 + cacheComponents) while others serve fine. Cure: `rm -rf apps/web/.next` before starting dev. Don't misread the 500s as an app bug — the prod build of the same source passes.

7. **`vercel link` writes into `apps/web/.env.local` — never `rm` that file.** The CLI appends a `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` and reports "✓ Updated .env.local", so the file looks like a linking artifact when it is actually Eric's pre-existing local env (2846 bytes, gitignored, unrecoverable from git). A subagent ran `rm -rf .vercel .env.local` as "cleanup" and destroyed it (2026-08-10).
   **How to apply:** clean up after `vercel link` with `rm -rf apps/web/.vercel` only. If the env file is already gone, restore it from the source repo — `cp -p /Users/eric/Projects/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev/apps/web/.env.local apps/web/` — which is where Conductor seeds workspace copies from; the OIDC token is ephemeral and regenerates. Tell agents driving Vercel not to touch `.env.local` at all.

8. **Preview deploys are SSO-protected**, so `curl`/Playwright get an auth wall. Vercel's Protection Bypass for Automation is the documented way through — but it mints secrets that must be revoked afterwards, so verify revocation in the dashboard rather than trusting an agent's report. (2026-08-10)

9. **Cache-invalidation behaviour does not reproduce in `next dev`.** `updateTag` in dev goes through a tiered cache handler (built-in front handler paired with the real one, `server/use-cache/handlers.js`), so a `use cache` entry written during a server action survives a reload — on Vercel it does not, because the tag's expiry watermark is stamped after the render that wrote it. Anything testing `use cache` / `updateTag` / revalidation semantics must be verified on a preview deploy; a clean dev run proves nothing. (2026-08-10, landing-page shell demo)

10. **Run `bun test` from inside the workspace dir, never the repo root.** Root `bun test` sweeps up every workspace's tests without their per-workspace `bunfig.toml` preloads, so `apps/web`'s fetch mocks are missing (`undefined is not an object (evaluating 'response.ok')` in email-validation tests) and mongodb throws an unhandled v8-snapshot error. The false failures look like regressions in files you never touched, and the test/file counts jump (189/30 → 208/34 was the tell, 2026-08-19). The usable gates: `cd apps/web && bun test`, or `turbo test --filter=web`.

Related: [[project_ts7_migration]]

content.text:
Done, both halves.

**The rewrite is live and verified.** Exhibit two now opens with "**But I already revalidated it.**" — and the intro answers it in the new opening beat: "You did, and it worked: the entry was gone the instant you called it, for every visitor at once. But a revalidation is a deletion with a hopeful name." The third paragraph closes the loop the title opens — "…the gap between those two moves is where you were standing when you said it." One self-correction during the voice pass: my draft's "the entry *died*" became "was gone," because §6's own evidence shows the kill-vocabulary losing a review before ("the shell you killed" → "the entry you expired"). 197 tests, lint clean, checked in the browser.

**The learnings, sorted by where they actually belong:**

- **`docs/voice.md`** got exactly what its own §9 permits — the two rejections today that no existing rule predicted, appended to §6's evidence: *(1)* a belief that resolves its own drama doesn't hook — catch the believer after the belief has failed them; *(2)* a genuinely new failure mode — the ritual aside was accurate and in-voice the day it shipped and was *obsoleted* by the demo growing a capability, so the three passes must re-run whenever the panel changes. Everything else stayed out of the guide, per its own bloat warning.
- **My persistent memory** (which is precisely the "somewhere" for improving how we work together — it loads into every future session) got three updates: the *brainstorming/design-rounds* memory rewritten to reflect what today proved (recommendation-led options with named trade-offs, short approval gates, your subtractive instinct, the four-audience test, and that trust escalates across rounds but the approval gate never lapses); a new *playground design language* memory (the fixed grammar, its principles, the migration state of demos 1/3–5, and the banked ideas — fruit as easter egg, comparison-row swatches, the two digest beats); and the env-quirks file gained the React DevTools false-error signature so no future session burns time re-diagnosing it.

You were right that voice.md was the wrong place for most of it — voice.md is the *site's* guide and should only ever learn from rejected lines; the collaboration and design-system knowledge now lives where it compounds across our sessions instead. If you'd ever rather have the design language as a checked-in sibling to `voice.md` (a `docs/design.md` other contributors could read), the memory file is written to convert almost verbatim — say the word.

Standing state: the chassis/swatch/title work and the voice.md append are uncommitted, and `14fadda8` + `93515eb3` are still local — all ready to commit and push together whenever you are.

content.text:
The fingerprint is now the literal value — six hex characters, a CSS color by construction. What changed to keep every layer honest:

- **`bake.ts`** mints `crypto.randomUUID().slice(0, 6)`, with the doc comment stating the design: the fingerprint *is* a color, nothing derived, nothing truncated.
- **`source.ts`** — the copy shown in the code drawer — updated in lockstep (`// the fingerprint — and a CSS color`), so the source a reader opens matches the behavior they're watching. That file silently lying would have been the worst version of the bug you caught.
- **`BakeSwatch`** drops its `slice` and renders `#${id}` raw — the truncation existed only because the id was longer than the value; now there's nothing to truncate.
- **Width reservations and tests** follow: the ghost placeholder is `000000`, and the pinned test fingerprints went six-char across both suites.

Verification is the satisfying part: the live run minted `#64f93b`, and the swatch's computed background came back `rgb(100, 249, 59)` — exactly `0x64 / 0xf9 / 0x3b`, byte for byte. A skeptic with a color picker now finds perfect agreement, which is the whole point of an unlabeled discovery on a page whose authority is checkability. 197 tests pass, lint clean.

One side effect worth naming: six characters is 16.7 million values instead of 4.3 billion. For a demo whose ids live one press at a time, collision odds are irrelevant — and the reducer's same-id fallback (built for the different-visitor race) already handles the freak case gracefully by showing the served line instead of a self-comparison.

# The instrument design guide

`voice.md`'s sibling: that guide governs what a visitor reads, this one
governs what they see and press. It exists for the same reason — the design
drifts, and it drifts toward decoration. Every element on a demo earns its
place by answering one question: does this contribute to clarity? The page's
feel is a developer environment, not a course platform. Engineer, not
student.

The audience is four people at once — an aspiring developer, a non-technical
visitor, a junior, a senior — and they get **one experience legible at all
levels, never per-level modes**. When a value needs to reach all four, encode
it redundantly (two channels, one display), don't fork the interface.

---

## 1. The fixed grammar

Every demo sits in the same chassis, zones in fixed positions — like a car's
cockpit or an editor's panes, a visitor who has used one instrument has used
them all:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● live                        SLOW MOTION ⭘ │  chrome: state left, view right
│                                              │
│  bake #64f93b                                │  the specimen
│  provenance rows · one narration caption     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ actions, in execution order ]              │  the deck
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ bake.ts + actions.ts       docs ↗ source ↗ │  reference bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Chrome, top-left — the state gauge.** `live` (cyan) at rest, `working`
  (amber) while any server round trip is out. One in-flight signal per
  instrument; this is it.
- **Chrome, top-right — view controls.** Mode switches (slow motion) live in
  the corner every editor keeps its view switches. Actions never live here.
  Empty when a demo has no alternate view.
- **Body — the specimen.** The observed value large, provenance rows as one
  aligned table, one narration caption. All describing text in one place.
- **Deck — actions only.** Execution order, left to right. When a flow has
  real sequence, the controls diagram it (numbered steps, an arrow, the later
  step dark until the earlier one fires).
- **Reference bar — the status bar every editor ends in.** The code drawer's
  disclosure left (source opens inside the chassis, native `<details>`, zero
  JS); `docs` and `source` links pinned right, positioned so clicking them
  never toggles the drawer. Row height mirrors the chrome header.

What the grammar deliberately lacks: a panel label (the intro prose names the
subject once) and a readout footer (the source in the drawer is the spec
plate — a reader who wants identifiers is the reader who opens it).

Outside the chassis: exhibit order rides in the eyebrow (`02 · caching &
revalidation`) where engineers read identifiers — no watermark chapter
numerals. Asides are set as `/* code comments */` in comment-gray mono,
because that is what they are.

## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and
settles. No silent updates, ever.

The React rule underneath: **client-owned state paints on the click frame;
only the server sync lives in a transition.** A mode flip inside the same
transition as its `router.refresh()` freezes the control until the round
trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

## 3. Copy and demo co-evolve

A demo that gains a capability can obsolete prose that was accurate the day
it shipped — voice.md's three passes check a line against the panel *as it
is*, so re-run them whenever the panel changes. (Evidence: voice.md §6,
2026-08-19.)

## 4. Migration state — 2026-08-19

Exhibit 02 (the rebake demo) is the reference implementation. Exhibits 01,
03, 04, 05 are on the legacy shape: `LivePanel` `label`/`readout` props,
standalone `CodeBlock`s, the old links row under the panel. Migration is
mostly mechanical per demo: compose a `ReferenceBar` with `CodeBlock
variant="bar"` into the panel's `references` slot, drop the label and
readout, move any mode switches to `viewControls`. The eyebrow and comment
asides are already global via `DemoSection`.

## 5. Banked

- The bake fingerprint is six hex characters — literally a CSS color — and
  the unlabeled `BakeSwatch` beside it renders that value. The discovery is
  intentional; the digest write-up is where it gets spelled out.
- Fruit/emoji hash encoding: rejected as primary (breaks instrument
  discipline), held as a possible easter-egg layer.
- Swatches in the machinery comparison rows: blocked until the string-based
  width-reservation (`StableSlot`) grows a JSX-safe design.
- Digest beats banked: the side-effect-runs-twice warning; the
  swatch-is-the-hash reveal.

## 6. Verification

`next dev` lies about cache semantics (`updateTag` entries survive reloads
that die on Vercel) — preview deploys are the truth-bench for anything
touching `use cache`. The React DevTools extension throws spurious "The
children should not have changed if we pass in the same set." errors on
transition commits here; stacks resolving to `chrome-extension://…` are the
extension's mirror desyncing, not an app bug.

## 7. Keeping this current

Same contract as voice.md §9: update on a decision that no rule here
predicted, never on a schedule. §1–§3 are the rules and should grow
reluctantly; §4–§6 are state and evidence — keep them dated, and correct
them when the code moves.

Eric's critique flags three rough spots in the demo 02 intro: the "revalidated/stale" phrasing drops in two unexplained concepts, "fingerprint" isn't visually grounded in the actual color swatch being shown, and the "where you were standing when you said it" line is just confusing as written.

He also suggests Brian Greene as a model for narrating abstract mechanisms — concrete everyday analogies, patient step-by-step escorting through the idea, "imagine..." framing, wonder without condescension. This feels like a new register worth adding to voice.md eventually, maybe as a fifth source alongside the existing four registers plus Ford's stance, specifically for mechanism explanations. For now though, the priority is just rewriting the intro itself.

I'm drafting the rewrite: fix the "both true" stumble by grounding "stale" earlier, and lean into the bakery metaphor already present in the demo's language — extending it so revalidating means throwing the loaf away and the shelf stays empty until the next order. It's concrete, walkable, and fits the existing voice, though I need to watch that it doesn't tip into cutesiness.

I should simplify the paradox language — instead of saying "revalidated and stale both true," just state it linearly: the deletion happened, nothing new baked, and the next visitor triggers the fresh version. I also need to ground the "fingerprint" concept in P2 before P3 relies on it, tying it to the stamp as this page's own cache entry shared by every visitor.

I'm finishing P2 with the stamp metaphor — one cache entry shared by every visitor, stamped with a fingerprint so you can tell one bake from the next, and pressing the button lands a fresh bake for everyone at once. For P3, I want to ground the ending more directly in the title quote rather than the oblique "where you were standing" — something like tying the gap between delete and request explicitly to "but I already revalidated it," and keeping "the fingerprint moves twice, not once" now that P2 has grounded what the fingerprint means.

I need to be careful about what the two moves actually are, though — it's not "deletion landing" and "refill arriving," it's the private render after expiry and then the shared render on the next fetch. The gap between those two renders is the stale window where the ticket sentence gets said. I'm drafting P3 to walk through running it in slow motion, watching the fingerprint move twice, and naming that gap as exactly where the sentence happens.

I'm also reworking P1 to drop the "both true" framing and instead land the point directly: a revalidation is just a deletion, nothing more, and the cache bakes a component's output once before handing out the same result to everyone.

I trim the triplet down to two beats instead — "you pulled the handle and the shelf emptied; no oven lit anywhere" — since three parallel clauses read too much like sequence narration. Drafting the final paragraph now: the revalidation bakes a component's output once and serves that copy to everyone, the cache tag is what you pull to discard it, pulling it empties the shelf without lighting any oven, and the fresh page only bakes when the next request asks for it.

Now I need to check P2 for redundancy since P1 already establishes "serves the same copy to everyone." I'll revise P2 to avoid repeating that and instead point directly at the stamp: "The stamp below is that copy — this page's own cache entry, wearing a six-character fingerprint so one bake is tellable from the next. Press the button and a fresh bake lands for all of them, in the time it takes the label to change back. It feels like one event." I also need to watch for "for every visitor at once" being reused from P1, and note that "static shell" phrasing got dropped when I tightened P1.

I like a more grounded alternative: "...it moves twice, not once. The gap between the two moves is the moment your ticket describes: the deletion done, the fresh bake not yet asked for." That ties back to the title concretely instead of leaning on abstract language.

I'm also checking that the fingerprint detail in P2 quietly sets up the six-character stamp so the reader can connect it without the color being named outright, and confirming the voice stays consistent with the escort verbs and concrete imagery established earlier.

The "fresh bake not yet asked for" phrasing holds up since the shared bake genuinely hasn't been requested yet in that gap, even though a private render occurred — the captions can carry that nuance while the intro stays simplified. I also want to note Eric's deliberate choice to invoke Brian Greene's register for narrating the abstract mechanism, per voice.md §1's list of register sources.

Since Eric explicitly endorsed this direction, it counts as a genuine new instrument worth adding rather than proposing separately — I'll draft a tight entry under §1, right after the Butterick spine, describing the Greene approach: escorting the reader through abstraction via a concrete scene, step by step, using words like "watch," "follow," "notice," with analogies that extend the exhibit's own metaphor rather than importing a foreign one.

I won't commit yet since Eric didn't ask for that — I'll apply the edit, verify it, and present the before/after clarity mapping for review, following the usual pattern where he reviews before approving a commit. I also want to double-check that the earlier phrase I removed from P2 still reads fine elsewhere in the panel, then write the actual edit.

content.text:
Your three stumbles diagnose precisely, and they share one root: the intro asks the reader to hold abstractions it never handed them. "Revalidated"/"stale" arrive as a logic puzzle before either word has a referent; "fingerprint" never gets attached to the `#64f93b` the reader is looking at; and "where you were standing" makes them solve a riddle at the exact moment they should feel the click. Brian Greene is the right prescription — his move is the *escorted walkthrough*: a concrete scene, extended one step at a time, with the reader told where to look ("watch", "follow") and the abstraction arriving only after its physical referent exists. And this exhibit already owns the perfect concrete scene: the bakery it's been speaking all along. The analogy shouldn't be imported; it should be *extended* — shelf and oven are one step past "bake."

The rewrite, stumble by stumble:

- **P1** keeps "a deletion with a hopeful name" (you kept it, it works) but replaces the both-true puzzle with the walkable scene: *pulling the handle empties the shelf and lights no oven*.
- **P2** grounds "fingerprint" the sentence before anyone needs it — "wearing a six-character fingerprint so you can tell one bake from the next" — which points the reader at `#64f93b` without spoiling the unlabeled color discovery.
- **P3** replaces the riddle with the direct tie: the gap is *the moment your ticket describes*.

The hero entrance animation compounds this: the readout fades in over roughly 1.1 seconds right when the fallback matters most, making it even less noticeable. And when the streamed content finally lands, it swaps in silently with no visual cue, violating the "no silent updates" rule.

My proposal: give the fallback a pulsing animation (respecting reduced-motion preferences) so it reads as pending rather than prose, and add an amber wash effect when the streamed line actually lands so the arrival feels noticeable — which fits the line's own message about streaming in just for the user. I'm working out the implementation, wrapping the streamed fragment in a span that triggers the landing animation on mount.

Since CSS animations fire whenever an element is inserted into the DOM, this works even before hydration, and it'll also re-trigger correctly on route refreshes since the streamed line re-renders with a new node each time — which actually feels right, since the line genuinely re-streamed. Both changes end up being compact, roughly one-line edits in hero-readout.tsx.

Eric's message is phrased as a question ("do we?"), so per the usual contract I should answer it directly and propose the fix rather than just implementing it outright — even though this fix is small enough I could apply it myself, I'll stick to assessment-mode and wait for his go-ahead.

content.text:
We do have one — it's just failing at its job. The line has a proper `Suspense` boundary with the fallback `waiting for the server…` (`opacity-50`, fixed `h-6` so the arrival never shifts layout), and under PPR that fallback is baked into the static shell, so it's on screen from the first paint until the stream delivers. You've almost certainly *seen* it without registering it — which is the actual defect. Three reasons it doesn't read as a loading state:

1. **Nothing moves.** It's faint static text that scans as a finished sentence, not as "in flight." Yesterday's design language codified exactly this standard — anything in flight says so visibly — and the hero readout predates that rule.
2. **It's hidden inside the entrance choreography.** The readout wrapper is `.ht-enter` with a 380ms delay plus a 700ms rise — the whole aside is still fading in during the first second, which is precisely the window when the fallback matters most. Faint text mid-fade is doubly invisible.
3. **The swap is silent.** When the streamed line lands, it just replaces the fallback — no announcement. That violates design.md's "no silent updates, ever," and it's especially ironic here, because *the arrival is the line's entire message*. A sentence that says "this line streamed in just for you" should be seen arriving.

The fix is two touches, both already in the grammar:

- **The fallback pulses** — `motion-safe:animate-pulse` on the existing span, keeping the static `opacity-50` as the reduced-motion base. Now it reads as pending.
- **The arrival gets the landing wash** — wrap `StreamedNow`'s output in a span with `.ht-land`, the same amber wash the bake stamp uses. Since it's a pure CSS mount animation, it fires the moment the streamed HTML is inserted, before hydration even runs. Bonus coherence: on a re-bake or refresh the line re-streams with a new timestamp, and the wash re-announces it — the readout starts obeying the same feedback rules as the instrument below it.

Copy stays as is — "waiting for the server…" is honest and in voice. Want me to apply the pair?

content.thinking:
Eric's pushing back on the premise — he's never actually experienced the revalidated-but-stale gap as a lived problem, since read-your-own-writes makes everything feel like one seamless event. The one place he did encounter the concept was through Vercel's observability, seeing MISS/STALE/HIT markers in logs and headers and wondering what they meant.

So I'm questioning whether the "but I already revalidated it" ticket framing is really the right hook, since it presupposes an edge case rather than the more common confusion developers hit: staring at cache headers and not understanding why something shows STALE when they thought it was fixed. That STALE state exists precisely because staleness-marking and refill are decoupled — which is the real, felt version of the two-events truth he's asking for.

Actually, the real belief underneath is "it's either cached or it isn't" — the binary hit/miss mental model that STALE shatters. That's the misconception: people don't expect a third state where something is expired but still served while fresh data bakes in the background, and that's exactly what the STALE badge in Vercel logs is naming. Now I need to check whether our demo actually demonstrates that third state.

Looking closer, our updateTag demo shows the gap as empty after expiry — a miss that triggers a rebuild — not a stale-serve. The STALE badge really belongs to the SWR pattern, where an entry past its revalidate window gets served anyway while refilling in the background. So I need to be careful: our demo proves expiry and refill are decoupled events, but it's not literally showing the stale-serve behavior — that's a different flavor of the same underlying gap. The honest way to bridge this is to frame both MISS and STALE as two different answers platforms give to the same gap between expiration and refill.

Now I'm thinking through title options for the piece, starting with something like "It's either cached or it isn't" — a plain-spoken statement of the binary mental model that the piece then detonates by introducing the third state.

I'm leaning toward that option since it keeps the existing intro mechanics intact: the demo reveals "there's a third thing," and the arc maps naturally from a single fused event (hit→hit) to three distinct events (expiry, gap, refill), with the gap itself being that third state. I'm starting to draft the intro paragraph around this belief-then-reveal structure.

I'm mapping out the three-paragraph structure: P1 breaks the binary and explains the mechanism, P2 captures the stamp/fused-press feeling, and P3 slows down to name the gap explicitly, tying it to real log vocabulary — MISS after a tag expiry, STALE served while a background refresh is still baking. I want to make sure both terms map precisely onto what Vercel's logs actually report.

The title change has ripple effects — the old "argument" ending in P3 gets cut since Eric rejected it, and "revalidated" fades from the title while the eyebrow and captions stay intact. I'm also rejecting another version of the opening line, "But I already revalidated it," because the misconception needs to be something developers actually live through via their logs, not just a plausible-sounding claim about the mechanism.

Checking this against the existing rule that a belief "has to be a sentence a developer has actually said" — the rejection actually confirms the rule worked correctly, since nobody really says that argument sentence given how RYOW makes it moot. So per the principle that a predicted failure means the document is working as intended, no rule change is needed here, just confirmation the existing guidance held.

Now I'm thinking about how to present this to Eric: lay out the diagnosis that RYOW hides the gap from users while the logs are the real lived touchpoint, propose the new belief "It's either cached or it isn't," sketch the arc, and tie in the observability bridge — then wait for his go-ahead before proceeding further.

I'm also noting his point about accidentally building an impure function or mutating data during a GET — that's actually exactly what the demo does on purpose, which the seam aside already covers.

Now I'm drafting concrete proposal copy so he can react to real lines: the title "It's either cached or it isn't," followed by an opening paragraph contrasting the binary hit/miss framing against the third word — stale — that broke it once the request logs spoke up, and explaining how `<use cache>` bakes a component's output into the page's static shell as one copy served to everyone.

I'm refining the ending — a cache tag is the handle that throws that copy away, emptying the shelf without lighting the oven, and the fresh page only bakes when the next request asks for one. I want to be precise that the gap between those two moments isn't itself a hit or miss; hit, miss, and stale are just where a request happens to land relative to that gap.

Wait, I need to be more precise about what actually breaks the binary here. The real lifecycle is fresh → stale-but-still-served → expired → refilled, and staleness is the state that truly defies "cached or not" — but my demo with updateTag only shows expiry and refill decoupling, not stale-serving. So the honest claim for this demo is narrower: what it actually proves is that clearing and filling aren't the same operation, not that there's some exotic third state of cached-ness.

That "not X, it's Y" framing works since X is the actual stated belief. For P3, I'm landing on: the fingerprint moves twice, not once, and that gap between moves is exactly why logs need a third word — a request landing there is an unexpected MISS, or worse, a stale serve while the fresh bake is still in progress.

I think it passes since it's explaining the reader's own observable logs using the mechanism already proven, though I should flag that P3 now carries two definitional claims beyond what the panel shows — defensible since they're the reader's own data, not invented. I'll keep the logs-tie in P3 rather than moving it to the aside, since the aside is doing a different job and shouldn't be churned. The "MISS you didn't expect" claim holds true for updateTag flows, and the title "It's either cached or it isn't" still reads as natural speech.

The opening beat answers the title's stance well, there's no collision with other title candidates, and the curly apostrophe is correct. I'm ready to present the proposal with the diagnosis, full draft, and a note on the voice.md discipline — no guide edit needed since the rule predicted this, I just misapplied it. Now I'll wait for the green light.

content.text:
You've falsified the premise, and the falsification is airtight: read-your-own-writes exists precisely so that *using* a site never exposes the gap — so the argument-with-the-page is an experience almost no developer has actually had. I dressed the mechanism up as a lived moment, but the mechanism hides itself from users by design. That was the §6 rule ("a sentence a developer has *actually said*") being violated by me, not a gap in the rule — so per §9 discipline, voice.md doesn't change this time; my application does.

Where developers *actually* meet this mechanism is exactly where you met it: **the logs.** `x-vercel-cache: HIT`, `MISS`, `STALE` — and the belief those three words detonate is the binary mental model everyone carries in: **a cache either has it or it doesn't.** "Why is this a MISS? I cached it." "What does STALE even mean — it's served *and* it's old?" The third word exists because expiry and refill are two events — the exact thing our panel proves. The demo doesn't need new mechanics; it needs the copy to route through the observability experience instead of a fictional support ticket.

Proposed title:

> **It's either cached or it isn't.**

Plain speech, genuinely believed, jargon-free enough for all four audiences — and the demo's whole choreography becomes its refutation. The arc:

**P1** — stance first, then the bakery walk survives intact: *"So did we — hit or miss, there or not. But 'cached' is not a state a page is in; it is a bake with a lifespan. `use cache` bakes a component's output into the page's static shell — one copy, served to everyone — and a cache tag is the handle you pull to throw that copy away. Pulling it empties the shelf and lights no oven. The fresh page is baked when the next request asks for one, and not a moment before."* (The "not X; it is Y" shape is legal here — X is literally the title.)

**P2** — unchanged: the stamp, the fingerprint, the fused press, "It feels like one event."

**P3** — the payoff lands in your logs instead of an argument: *"It is three. Flip the switch and run it again in slow motion — the panel narrates each event as it happens. # The instrument design guide

`voice.md`'s sibling: that guide governs what a visitor reads, this one
governs what they see and press. It exists for the same reason — the design
drifts, and it drifts toward decoration. Every element on a demo earns its
place by answering one question: does this contribute to clarity? The page's
feel is a developer environment, not a course platform. Engineer, not
student.

The audience is four people at once — an aspiring developer, a non-technical
visitor, a junior, a senior — and they get **one experience legible at all
levels, never per-level modes**. When a value needs to reach all four, encode
it redundantly (two channels, one display), don't fork the interface.

---

## 1. The fixed grammar

Every demo sits in the same chassis, zones in fixed positions — like a car's
cockpit or an editor's panes, a visitor who has used one instrument has used
them all:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● live                        SLOW MOTION ⭘ │  chrome: state left, view right
│                                              │
│  bake #64f93b                                │  the specimen
│  provenance rows · one narration caption     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ actions, in execution order ]              │  the deck
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ bake.ts + actions.ts       docs ↗ source ↗ │  reference bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Chrome, top-left — the state gauge.** `live` (cyan) at rest, `working`
  (amber) while any server round trip is out. One in-flight signal per
  instrument; this is it.
- **Chrome, top-right — view controls.** Mode switches (slow motion) live in
  the corner every editor keeps its view switches. Actions never live here.
  Empty when a demo has no alternate view.
- **Body — the specimen.** The observed value large, provenance rows as one
  aligned table, one narration caption. All describing text in one place.
- **Deck — actions only.** Execution order, left to right. When a flow has
  real sequence, the controls diagram it (numbered steps, an arrow, the later
  step dark until the earlier one fires).
- **Reference bar — the status bar every editor ends in.** The code drawer's
  disclosure left (source opens inside the chassis, native `<details>`, zero
  JS); `docs` and `source` links pinned right, positioned so clicking them
  never toggles the drawer. Row height mirrors the chrome header.

What the grammar deliberately lacks: a panel label (the intro prose names the
subject once) and a readout footer (the source in the drawer is the spec
plate — a reader who wants identifiers is the reader who opens it).

Outside the chassis: exhibit order rides in the eyebrow (`02 · caching &
revalidation`) where engineers read identifiers — no watermark chapter
numerals. Asides are set as `/* code comments */` in comment-gray mono,
because that is what they are.

## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and
settles. No silent updates, ever.

The React rule underneath: **client-owned state paints on the click frame;
only the server sync lives in a transition.** A mode flip inside the same
transition as its `router.refresh()` freezes the control until the round
trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

## 3. Copy and demo co-evolve

A demo that gains a capability can obsolete prose that was accurate the day
it shipped — voice.md's three passes check a line against the panel *as it
is*, so re-run them whenever the panel changes. (Evidence: voice.md §6,
2026-08-19.)

## 4. Migration state — 2026-08-19

Exhibit 02 (the rebake demo) is the reference implementation. Exhibits 01,
03, 04, 05 are on the legacy shape: `LivePanel` `label`/`readout` props,
standalone `CodeBlock`s, the old links row under the panel. Migration is
mostly mechanical per demo: compose a `ReferenceBar` with `CodeBlock
variant="bar"` into the panel's `references` slot, drop the label and
readout, move any mode switches to `viewControls`. The eyebrow and comment
asides are already global via `DemoSection`.

## 5. Banked

- The bake fingerprint is six hex characters — literally a CSS color — and
  the unlabeled `BakeSwatch` beside it renders that value. The discovery is
  intentional; the digest write-up is where it gets spelled out.
- Fruit/emoji hash encoding: rejected as primary (breaks instrument
  discipline), held as a possible easter-egg layer.
- Swatches in the machinery comparison rows: blocked until the string-based
  width-reservation (`StableSlot`) grows a JSX-safe design.
- Digest beats banked: the side-effect-runs-twice warning; the
  swatch-is-the-hash reveal.

## 6. Verification

`next dev` lies about cache semantics (`updateTag` entries survive reloads
that die on Vercel) — preview deploys are the truth-bench for anything
touching `use cache`. The React DevTools extension throws spurious "The
children should not have changed if we pass in the same set." errors on
transition commits here; stacks resolving to `chrome-extension://…` are the
extension's mirror desyncing, not an app bug.

## 7. Keeping this current

Same contract as voice.md §9: update on a decision that no rule here
predicted, never on a schedule. §1–§3 are the rules and should grow
reluctantly; §4–§6 are state and evidence — keep them dated, and correct
them when the code moves.

Both threads converge nicely. Proposal first, then the wording call you asked for.

## Integrating the badges: the pipeline grows its output

The panel can't honestly badge *arbitrary* requests — the visitor's own page load might have been `PRERENDER`, `HIT`, or `REVALIDATED`, and the app never sees which (the CDN assigns it). But the **refill request is badge-able by rule**: tag-based deletion ⇒ the asking request logs `REVALIDATED` — that's platform behavior, verified in our logs yesterday and this morning. So the one place a badge can live truthfully is as the *result* of the machinery run.

And there's a natural slot for it: the deck already diagrams the sequence — `1 Expire the entry → 2 Ask for the page`. When the reveal lands, the diagram completes with its output node:

```
[ 1 Expire the entry ]  →  [ 2 Ask for the page ]  →  REVALIDATED · TAG-BASED DELETION
```

A small bordered mono chip, styled like the observability badge, appearing only in the machinery view's revealed state (space reserved invisibly, same no-hop pattern as everything else). The intro's P3 makes the verbal claim; the deck *shows* it at the moment it becomes true; nothing is said twice. The tag itself is already integrated — it's the literal string in the drawer (`cacheTag("landing-shell")`) and "tag-based deletion" names the connection the way the log does. This needs one amendment to design.md's deck rule: the deck may end in a **result chip — output, never input** — which I'd argue completes the "controls diagram the mechanism" principle rather than bending it.

## The "hash above" wording

You're right it must change — but I'd recommend **"the bake above"** over "the color above" for these two lines, because both sentences are about what the cache *keeps*, and the cache keeps bakes; the color is the bake's name. "The color above was rendered… so the cache will not keep it" makes the color the cached object, which quietly un-teaches P2. So:

- expired caption → "**the bake above** was rendered before your expiry landed, so the cache will not keep it…"
- settling detail → "**the bake above** is still the private one — its replacement is in flight"

"Bake" is also already the established referent everywhere else ("the bake above is what every visitor gets," "#1f41b6 is the bake above"). Where "color" *does* earn a place is where the reader is told what to watch — P3's "Watch the fingerprint: it moves twice" could become "**Watch the color: it changes twice**," which privileges the glance channel the swatch exists for. I'd make that swap too, but it's your call — P2 grounds "fingerprint," so either referent is now safe.

Scope if you green-light all of it: the two caption strings + tests, the result chip in `rebake-panel.tsx`, optionally the P3 watch-line, and the design.md deck amendment. Go?

# The instrument design guide

`voice.md`'s sibling: that guide governs what a visitor reads, this one
governs what they see and press. It exists for the same reason — the design
drifts, and it drifts toward decoration. Every element on a demo earns its
place by answering one question: does this contribute to clarity? The page's
feel is a developer environment, not a course platform. Engineer, not
student.

The audience is four people at once — an aspiring developer, a non-technical
visitor, a junior, a senior — and they get **one experience legible at all
levels, never per-level modes**. When a value needs to reach all four, encode
it redundantly (two channels, one display), don't fork the interface.

---

## 1. The fixed grammar

Every demo sits in the same chassis, zones in fixed positions — like a car's
cockpit or an editor's panes, a visitor who has used one instrument has used
them all:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● live                        SLOW MOTION ⭘ │  chrome: state left, view right
│                                              │
│  bake #64f93b                                │  the specimen
│  provenance rows · one narration caption     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ actions, in execution order ]              │  the deck
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ bake.ts + actions.ts       docs ↗ source ↗ │  reference bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Chrome, top-left — the state gauge.** `live` (cyan) at rest, `working`
  (amber) while any server round trip is out. One in-flight signal per
  instrument; this is it.
- **Chrome, top-right — view controls.** Mode switches (slow motion) live in
  the corner every editor keeps its view switches. Actions never live here.
  Empty when a demo has no alternate view.
- **Body — the specimen.** The observed value large, provenance rows as one
  aligned table, one narration caption. All describing text in one place.
- **Deck — actions only.** Execution order, left to right. When a flow has
  real sequence, the controls diagram it (numbered steps, an arrow, the later
  step dark until the earlier one fires).
- **Reference bar — the status bar every editor ends in.** The code drawer's
  disclosure left (source opens inside the chassis, native `<details>`, zero
  JS); `docs` and `source` links pinned right, positioned so clicking them
  never toggles the drawer. Row height mirrors the chrome header.

What the grammar deliberately lacks: a panel label (the intro prose names the
subject once) and a readout footer (the source in the drawer is the spec
plate — a reader who wants identifiers is the reader who opens it).

Outside the chassis: exhibit order rides in the eyebrow (`02 · caching &
revalidation`) where engineers read identifiers — no watermark chapter
numerals. Asides are set as `/* code comments */` in comment-gray mono,
because that is what they are.

## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and
settles. No silent updates, ever.

The React rule underneath: **client-owned state paints on the click frame;
only the server sync lives in a transition.** A mode flip inside the same
transition as its `router.refresh()` freezes the control until the round
trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

## 3. Copy and demo co-evolve

A demo that gains a capability can obsolete prose that was accurate the day
it shipped — voice.md's three passes check a line against the panel *as it
is*, so re-run them whenever the panel changes. (Evidence: voice.md §6,
2026-08-19.)

## 4. Migration state — 2026-08-19

Exhibit 02 (the rebake demo) is the reference implementation. Exhibits 01,
03, 04, 05 are on the legacy shape: `LivePanel` `label`/`readout` props,
standalone `CodeBlock`s, the old links row under the panel. Migration is
mostly mechanical per demo: compose a `ReferenceBar` with `CodeBlock
variant="bar"` into the panel's `references` slot, drop the label and
readout, move any mode switches to `viewControls`. The eyebrow and comment
asides are already global via `DemoSection`.

## 5. Banked

- The bake fingerprint is six hex characters — literally a CSS color — and
  the unlabeled `BakeSwatch` beside it renders that value. The discovery is
  intentional; the digest write-up is where it gets spelled out.
- Fruit/emoji hash encoding: rejected as primary (breaks instrument
  discipline), held as a possible easter-egg layer.
- Swatches in the machinery comparison rows: blocked until the string-based
  width-reservation (`StableSlot`) grows a JSX-safe design.
- Digest beats banked: the side-effect-runs-twice warning; the
  swatch-is-the-hash reveal.

## 6. Verification

`next dev` lies about cache semantics (`updateTag` entries survive reloads
that die on Vercel) — preview deploys are the truth-bench for anything
touching `use cache`.

The verified badge sequence for the rebake flow on Vercel (2026-08-20,
preview logs): `PRERENDER` on first visit → `HIT` → `BYPASS` for the action
POST → `REVALIDATED`, reason "Tag-based deletion", for the request that
refills. `updateTag` never produces `STALE` (that badge is
stale-while-revalidate: `revalidateTag` or a lapsed `cacheLife` window), and
the tag-deletion miss is labeled `REVALIDATED`, not `MISS`. Copy that names
log badges must match this. The React DevTools extension throws spurious "The
children should not have changed if we pass in the same set." errors on
transition commits here; stacks resolving to `chrome-extension://…` are the
extension's mirror desyncing, not an app bug.

## 7. Keeping this current

Same contract as voice.md §9: update on a decision that no rule here
predicted, never on a schedule. §1–§3 are the rules and should grow
reluctantly; §4–§6 are state and evidence — keep them dated, and correct
them when the code moves.

There are two things to address: committing the changes (not pushing, just committing), and a UI timing question about whether the second button becomes clickable too early—right after clicking "Expire the entry" but before the action's response has actually landed. I'm tracing through the rebake flow to understand the current mechanics: handleRebake triggers startRebake, which awaits the rebake call before dispatching the expired state, and I'm checking how the fetchable flag is derived from state to see if there's a gap worth closing.

I'm working through the timing more carefully—the action's promise resolution and the private render update both come from the same response, but React may apply them in separate stages, so the dispatch marking the entry as expired could land slightly before or after the re-render that updates the stamp, which is the crux of whether there's actually a visible gap.

I'm trying to figure out whether the dispatch and the RSC payload application commit in the same paint — if they do, there's no capture bug, just a timing/UX concern. But the dev screenshots actually show the old hash still displayed while "Re-baking…" is in flight, and the rebake-state.ts comment confirms the private render hasn't returned yet at expiry time, meaning the stamp shown is stale.

So if a user clicks step 2 during that window, handleFetch captures the still-old hash as the "private" id, which produces a false claim — the panel would say that old hash was "yours alone" when it was actually the shared bake everyone saw, not a private one. That's a genuine lie in the UI, not just a speed issue.

One fix is to close the gap entirely: keep step 2 disabled until the private render has actually landed, which I could detect by recording the id at the moment of expiry and only re-enabling once the current id changes away from it — though I need to think through edge cases like another visitor refilling during that same window.

Since new ids are random 6-hex values, a fresh render will almost always differ from the expired one, so gating on "currentId !== expiredFromId" is clean and testable, with the reducer simply recording that id from the dispatch payload. The existing isRebaking lock already covers step 1 during the flight, so this gate just adds the requirement that the render has visibly landed before step 2 unlocks, meaning in practice it enables one paint after the stamp flips.

I'm weighing whether to close this gap or leave it intentional — leaving it lets fast users skip seeing the private render, but that makes the comparison dishonest since we can't capture the private id before it actually renders client-side. So the right call is to close it: gate step 2 on the private render having landed, which also makes the expired caption's claim ("the bake above was rendered before your expiry landed") actually true at the moment it lights up.

Now I'm working out the implementation — the expired phase needs to track the id that was on screen at expiry time, and the fetch-gating check needs to compare against the current id to confirm the render has moved past it. But I realize the settle-check used elsewhere in the toggle handler shouldn't use this same stricter condition, since any unanswered expiry needs settling regardless of whether the render landed — so I need two separate conditions: one for the button's fetch gate, and one for the settle logic.

I'm splitting this into a plain gap-open check based on phase alone for settling, and a new stricter check that also compares the current id against the id stored at expiry for the fetch button. I'm updating the reducer so the expired action stores that id, updating the test helpers and assertions to match, and adding a new test confirming the ask stays disabled until the id changes to reflect the new render.

I'm tracing through the handler closure to confirm it captures the right id at click time, checking that the toggle-off edge case during an unlanded expiry still triggers a refresh correctly, and confirming the deck's disabled prop and fused mode are unaffected. Now I'm looking at whether the expired caption copy is still accurate in the brief window before the new render actually lands.

The caption still holds since the displayed bake genuinely predates the expiry even during that gap, so no fix needed there. I also want to make sure step 2 shows as visibly disabled rather than hidden during that blink, then move to committing the current batch of changes before tackling the gap fix as separate follow-up work — since this turned out to be a real correctness bug producing a false comparison rather than just a UX nit, I should give a clear recommendation on whether to close or keep it intentionally.

The answer is clear: close it. I'll implement the fix alongside the commit since his question was a direct either/or about this exact change, and the "keep" option doesn't hold up once you see it produces a falsehood in a demo whose whole point is honesty.

The settle path deliberately keeps the looser check (any open gap owes a refresh on the way out, landed or not). The reducer stays pure, the gate has its own test with the failure mode documented in its comment, and the browser run confirmed the button never lit while the old fingerprint was still up — enabling exactly one paint after the private render arrived.

name: project-env-quirks
description: "Machine/env quirks on Eric's Mac that bite headless agent sessions (docker pulls, biome gate)"
metadata:

Two environment quirks hit during the knowledge-hub build (2026-07-11):

1. **`docker pull` hangs forever in headless sessions.** `~/.docker/config.json` has `credsStore: "desktop"` plus a Docker Scout hook on `pull`; the credential helper blocks on macOS Keychain without a UI. Even `docker run` hangs at "Unable to find image locally".
   **How to apply:** `mkdir -p /tmp/docker-nocreds && echo '{}' > /tmp/docker-nocreds/config.json`, then `DOCKER_CONFIG=/tmp/docker-nocreds docker pull …` — completes in seconds. `docker ps`/`exec`/`run` (with image present) work normally.

2. **Biome gate (ultracite v7 extends paths): fixed per-branch, not repo-wide.** biome.jsonc must extend `ultracite/biome/*` (v7 layout), not the v5-era `ultracite/core|react|next`; check/fix scripts must run the local ultracite pin, never `@latest`. Applied on Kheirah/agent-knowledge-hub-design (484e1a0 + 26327a7, 2026-07-11) and independently re-derived on Kheirah/continue-prev-task (fe73b90, 2026-07-12) — branches cut before those commits will still show "Could not resolve ultracite/core"; apply the same two-line fix. Repo-wide pre-existing findings remain (hundreds; scoped `bunx biome check <path>` is the usable gate for new work). The masterclass exhibit dir is mechanically clean as of fe73b90 (~36 judgment-rule findings left: noJsxPropsBind, noExportedImports, index keys).
   **Zombie dirty files:** entire.io (manual-commit strategy) snapshots uncommitted changes to a shadow branch and re-applies them post-commit ("carried forward remaining files") — a plain `git checkout --` of unwanted noise gets silently undone at the next commit. Cure: `git checkout -- <files> && entire clean --force` (drops the HEAD shadow branch + session carry-forward state; committed checkpoint history is unaffected).
   Also: Biome's `useSortedKeys` assist auto-sorts object keys on `--write` — it silently reorders semantically-ordered literals (MongoDB compound-index key specs). Guard such files with `// biome-ignore-all assist/source/useSortedKeys: …`.

3. **Vercel:** hasToggle.dev deploys as project `has-toggle-dev-web` under team scope `spiritsdontfly` (not the default `kheirahs-projects`, not `forsuxess`). Use `vercel ls/inspect --scope spiritsdontfly`; `vercel inspect --logs <url>` pulls build logs without switching scope. (2026-07-24)

4. **Bun override staleness:** after adding a root `overrides` entry, plain `bun install` updates `bun.lock` but can leave stale `.bun` store symlinks (nested dep still resolving to the old version). `rm -rf node_modules && bun install` is required for the override to actually take effect. (2026-07-24, radix-slot pin)

5. **The `web` app's locale-prefixed URLs 500 in dev.** `http://localhost:3001/en/learn/...` dies in middleware (`[NEMO] Middleware execution failed`); the unprefixed `http://localhost:3001/learn/...` serves fine. Use the unprefixed path when driving the site in a browser or the masterclass page looks broken when it isn't. `curl` also 500s on both (the middleware chain needs real browser headers) — verify with Playwright/Chrome DevTools, not curl. Next 16 also refuses to start a second dev server for the same project dir ("Run kill <pid> to stop it"), so reuse Eric's running server on 3001 rather than starting your own. (2026-07-25)

6. **Shared `.next` dir: `next build` then `next dev` corrupts some routes.** Running dev after a prod build in the same `apps/web/.next` produces `SyntaxError: Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON` and 500s on a subset of routes (hit the nuqs-using learn pages, 2026-07-31, Next 16.2 + cacheComponents) while others serve fine. Cure: `rm -rf apps/web/.next` before starting dev. Don't misread the 500s as an app bug — the prod build of the same source passes.

7. **`vercel link` writes into `apps/web/.env.local` — never `rm` that file.** The CLI appends a `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` and reports "✓ Updated .env.local", so the file looks like a linking artifact when it is actually Eric's pre-existing local env (2846 bytes, gitignored, unrecoverable from git). A subagent ran `rm -rf .vercel .env.local` as "cleanup" and destroyed it (2026-08-10).
   **How to apply:** clean up after `vercel link` with `rm -rf apps/web/.vercel` only. If the env file is already gone, restore it from the source repo — `cp -p /Users/eric/Projects/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev/apps/web/.env.local apps/web/` — which is where Conductor seeds workspace copies from; the OIDC token is ephemeral and regenerates. Tell agents driving Vercel not to touch `.env.local` at all.

8. **Preview deploys are SSO-protected**, so `curl`/Playwright get an auth wall. Vercel's Protection Bypass for Automation is the documented way through — but it mints secrets that must be revoked afterwards, so verify revocation in the dashboard rather than trusting an agent's report. (2026-08-10)

9. **Cache-invalidation behaviour does not reproduce in `next dev`.** `updateTag` in dev goes through a tiered cache handler (built-in front handler paired with the real one, `server/use-cache/handlers.js`), so a `use cache` entry written during a server action survives a reload — on Vercel it does not, because the tag's expiry watermark is stamped after the render that wrote it. Anything testing `use cache` / `updateTag` / revalidation semantics must be verified on a preview deploy; a clean dev run proves nothing. (2026-08-10, landing-page shell demo)

10. **React DevTools extension throws spurious console errors on the rebake demo.** "The children should not have changed if we pass in the same set." with a stack entirely inside `chrome-extension://…/installHook.js` — the extension's fiber-mirror desyncs on transition commits with RSC children props + keyed remounts. Not an app bug: absent in extension-free browsers, string doesn't exist in React/Next/Radix bundles. Diagnose via `apps/web/.next/dev/logs/next-development.log` (timestamps are server *uptime*, not wall clock). (2026-08-19)

11. **Run `bun test` from inside the workspace dir, never the repo root.** Root `bun test` sweeps up every workspace's tests without their per-workspace `bunfig.toml` preloads, so `apps/web`'s fetch mocks are missing (`undefined is not an object (evaluating 'response.ok')` in email-validation tests) and mongodb throws an unhandled v8-snapshot error. The false failures look like regressions in files you never touched, and the test/file counts jump (189/30 → 208/34 was the tell, 2026-08-19). The usable gates: `cd apps/web && bun test`, or `turbo test --filter=web`.

Related: [[project_ts7_migration]]

# The instrument design guide

`voice.md`'s sibling: that guide governs what a visitor reads, this one
governs what they see and press. It exists for the same reason — the design
drifts, and it drifts toward decoration. Every element on a demo earns its
place by answering one question: does this contribute to clarity? The page's
feel is a developer environment, not a course platform. Engineer, not
student.

The audience is four people at once — an aspiring developer, a non-technical
visitor, a junior, a senior — and they get **one experience legible at all
levels, never per-level modes**. When a value needs to reach all four, encode
it redundantly (two channels, one display), don't fork the interface.

---

## 1. The fixed grammar

Every demo sits in the same chassis, zones in fixed positions — like a car's
cockpit or an editor's panes, a visitor who has used one instrument has used
them all:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● live                        SLOW MOTION ⭘ │  chrome: state left, view right
│                                              │
│  bake #64f93b                                │  the specimen
│  provenance rows · one narration caption     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ actions, in execution order ]              │  the deck
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ bake.ts + actions.ts       docs ↗ source ↗ │  reference bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Chrome, top-left — the state gauge.** `live` (cyan) at rest, `working`
  (amber) while any server round trip is out. One in-flight signal per
  instrument; this is it.
- **Chrome, top-right — view controls.** Mode switches (slow motion) live in
  the corner every editor keeps its view switches. Actions never live here.
  Empty when a demo has no alternate view.
- **Body — the specimen.** The observed value large, provenance rows as one
  aligned table, one narration caption. All describing text in one place.
- **Deck — actions only.** Execution order, left to right. When a flow has
  real sequence, the controls diagram it (numbered steps, an arrow, the later
  step dark until the earlier one fires). A deck may end in a **result chip —
  output, never input** — when the platform's own label for the sequence's
  outcome is knowable by rule (exhibit 02: `revalidated · tag-based
  deletion`, the badge Vercel files the refill under).
- **Reference bar — the status bar every editor ends in.** The code drawer's
  disclosure left (source opens inside the chassis, native `<details>`, zero
  JS); `docs` and `source` links pinned right, positioned so clicking them
  never toggles the drawer. Row height mirrors the chrome header.

What the grammar deliberately lacks: a panel label (the intro prose names the
subject once) and a readout footer (the source in the drawer is the spec
plate — a reader who wants identifiers is the reader who opens it).

Outside the chassis: exhibit order rides in the eyebrow (`02 · caching &
revalidation`) where engineers read identifiers — no watermark chapter
numerals. Asides are set as `/* code comments */` in comment-gray mono,
because that is what they are.

## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and
settles. No silent updates, ever.

The React rule underneath: **client-owned state paints on the click frame;
only the server sync lives in a transition.** A mode flip inside the same
transition as its `router.refresh()` freezes the control until the round
trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

## 3. Copy and demo co-evolve

A demo that gains a capability can obsolete prose that was accurate the day
it shipped — voice.md's three passes check a line against the panel *as it
is*, so re-run them whenever the panel changes. (Evidence: voice.md §6,
2026-08-19.)

## 4. Migration state — 2026-08-19

Exhibit 02 (the rebake demo) is the reference implementation. Exhibits 01,
03, 04, 05 are on the legacy shape: `LivePanel` `label`/`readout` props,
standalone `CodeBlock`s, the old links row under the panel. Migration is
mostly mechanical per demo: compose a `ReferenceBar` with `CodeBlock
variant="bar"` into the panel's `references` slot, drop the label and
readout, move any mode switches to `viewControls`. The eyebrow and comment
asides are already global via `DemoSection`.

## 5. Banked

- The bake fingerprint is six hex characters — literally a CSS color — and
  the unlabeled `BakeSwatch` beside it renders that value. The discovery is
  intentional; the digest write-up is where it gets spelled out.
- Fruit/emoji hash encoding: rejected as primary (breaks instrument
  discipline), held as a possible easter-egg layer.
- Swatches in the machinery comparison rows: blocked until the string-based
  width-reservation (`StableSlot`) grows a JSX-safe design.
- Digest beats banked: the side-effect-runs-twice warning; the
  swatch-is-the-hash reveal.

## 6. Verification

`next dev` lies about cache semantics (`updateTag` entries survive reloads
that die on Vercel) — preview deploys are the truth-bench for anything
touching `use cache`.

The verified badge sequence for the rebake flow on Vercel (2026-08-20,
preview logs): `PRERENDER` on first visit → `HIT` → `BYPASS` for the action
POST → `REVALIDATED`, reason "Tag-based deletion", for the request that
refills. `updateTag` never produces `STALE` (that badge is
stale-while-revalidate: `revalidateTag` or a lapsed `cacheLife` window), and
the tag-deletion miss is labeled `REVALIDATED`, not `MISS`. Copy that names
log badges must match this. The React DevTools extension throws spurious "The
children should not have changed if we pass in the same set." errors on
transition commits here; stacks resolving to `chrome-extension://…` are the
extension's mirror desyncing, not an app bug.

## 7. Keeping this current

Same contract as voice.md §9: update on a decision that no rule here
predicted, never on a schedule. §1–§3 are the rules and should grow
reluctantly; §4–§6 are state and evidence — keep them dated, and correct
them when the code moves.

content.text:
The migration is complete — all five exhibits now speak the same grammar, verified in the browser, with every gate green (198 tests, typecheck, lint). Eight files changed, uncommitted for your review.

**What each demo became:**

- **01 (boundary):** cards as specimen, plus a new narration line carrying the old readout's one non-redundant fact — "props cross the boundary as serialized data — the import graph decides which side a component runs on." Its two source files join into a single drawer (`server-card.tsx + client-card.tsx`), same pattern as the shell's.
- **03 (stream):** the rerun control moved to the deck with its own Suspense boundary (it reads the URL — runtime data), rows stream in the body. Its readout was fully redundant and died without replacement.
- **04 (mutation):** references bar only — and a deliberate non-move: the form **stays in the body**, because a form wired straight to a Server Action *is* the exhibit's subject, and filing it under instrument controls would misrepresent the lesson. Same reasoning keeps demo 01's click-me button in the specimen.
- **05 (image):** the deepest cut — `OgDemo` now owns its instrument, so the gauge genuinely flips to WORKING during the fetch (verified by polling), the title form is the deck, and the Satori facts became the narration line, honoring voice.md's "implementation limits read as specification" rule. There's also a pleasing recursion in the screenshot: the generated OG card contains its own tiny LIVE header, so the instrument now displays a picture of its own chrome.

**Legacy deleted, not deprecated:** `LivePanel` lost `label`/`readout`, `DemoSection` lost the links row and its `docs`/`sourcePath` props, `CodeBlock` collapsed to the frameless bar form (its standalone frame, the `variant` prop, and the now-dead `.shiki[title]` CSS all removed). Nothing on the page can regress to the old shape because the old shape no longer exists.

**One honest gap, recorded in design.md §4:** demo 03's gauge stays static — its in-flight signal is the row skeletons plus the rerun button's "Streaming…" label, which is real feedback but not the gauge; wiring it properly needs a client panel owner, noted for whenever that's worth doing. The design.md migration section now records completion and the three judgment calls (specimen-vs-control, narration-vs-cut, gauge wiring) so the next exhibit inherits the reasoning, not just the layout.

Ready to commit — my suggested split is two: the migration itself, then the legacy teardown. Say the word.

10:entire.io (CLI, hooks in `.claude/settings.json`) captures Claude Code sessions in this repo. As of 2026-07-11, checkpoints push to the **private** repo `hasToggle/hasToggle.dev-checkpoints` via `strategy_options.checkpoint_remote` in `.entire/settings.json` — NOT to origin. The old `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch was deleted from the public hasToggle.dev repo (full history migrated, SHA c84573f).
12:**Why:** Vercel (team spiritsdontfly, project has-toggle-dev-web, root directory `apps/web`) auto-deploys every pushed branch. The checkpoints branch has no `apps/web` → fails at `build-container-init` with `NOW_SANDBOX_WORKER_ROOTDIR_NOT_EXIST` **before the Ignored Build Step runs** — no ignore command can ever catch it. Every clone/worktree needs the merged `.entire/settings.json` (or run `entire configure --checkpoint-remote github:hasToggle/hasToggle.dev-checkpoints`). The four `apps/*/vercel.json` carry `git.deploymentEnabled: {"entire/*": false, "entire/**": false}` as defense for shadow branches. Known dead config: `ignoreCommand: node scripts/skip-ci.js` references a script that never existed (since initial commit) — exit 1 → every push builds. Related: [[project-env-quirks]]
