content.thinking:
I'm examining Eric's pushback on the hero footnote, checking whether the line does its job as the asterisk that substantiates "Watch it run" without deflating the claim — it needs to hand over concrete receipts like what to press and where the code lives.

The GIF anecdote fails the same test as the earlier "already revalidated it" line: it's a manufactured relatable moment rather than the reader's actual in-the-moment question, and it punches at unnamed third parties, which voice.md explicitly flags as a rejected move. The "So have we" stance line only works if it's propping up that flawed anecdote, so the fix is to cut the GIF bit and let the footnote point straight to the demos answering back and the code sitting one click away.

The hero readout right under the asterisk already shows the bake id and a line that streamed in live just for the visitor — so the asterisk could literally point at that readout as the proof. I'm drafting a couple of options: one that stays purely receipts-focused ("press it, source is one click down"), avoiding any internal jargon like "instrument" that the page doesn't use publicly, and another that explicitly names the readout below as evidence — one line baked before arrival, one streamed live — tying the asterisk directly to that visible proof.

I'm also recalling the old pre-redesign footnote, which said something like "run it yourself, everything answers when pressed, view source whenever you like — skepticism is the correct instinct," before it got replaced during the audit with the GIF version that added more stance. That old line was good but slightly flattering toward the reader by validating their skepticism. Now I'm trying a new draft that keeps the invitation to verify without manufacturing an anecdote — something like "run it and see, every demo answers when pressed, the source is one click down, even the prompts that built this page are public" — and testing a self-deprecating stance like "if you don't believe a landing page, good, neither do we" to keep the skepticism internal rather than flattering the reader.

But I notice this risks overlapping with the hero's existing aside, "Nothing on this page is a mockup. We checked twice," which already does the fourth-wall skepticism move — the footnote shouldn't repeat that joke. So I'm simplifying toward pure receipts: three terse, checkable pointers — the demos run live, the source is one click away, and the prompts that built the page are public — closing with an imperative like "believe none of it until you've pressed something," which drives action toward the CTA.

This matches the length of the hover card text, good. But I'm remembering Eric's usual pattern: he wants a diagnosis plus options, not just a final answer — so I should name the three failures in this draft, tie them to today's lesson, then offer two alternatives with a recommendation. I'm also flagging that this is now the third instance of a manufactured-lived-moment problem, which might mean it belongs in voice.md as a standing rule, since the GIF anecdote claims a shared experience that wasn't actually shared.

content.text:
It doesn't fit, and I can say precisely why — the line fails on three counts, two of which the guide itself already prosecuted:

1. **It's a manufactured shared experience** — the same failure class as "But I already revalidated it." Has anyone *actually* opened a live demo that turned out to be a GIF and carried the wound? Maybe once, vaguely. It's plausible-not-lived, and yesterday taught us that difference is fatal: relatability you invent reads as marketing doing an impression of empathy.
2. **It punches at third parties.** voice.md §1's own audit removed "Most landing pages hide that part" for exactly this — and the GIF anecdote is the same move wearing a costume: spending our footnote on other sites' sins. The stance rule wants us *inside* the diagnosis, not aiming it elsewhere.
3. **It deflects when it should substantiate.** §3 is explicit: the asterisk hands over receipts — what to press, what to read, how to check. Only the last sentence does that job; the first two are throat-clearing.

And the receipts got much better this week: every panel now carries its source one click down in its own reference bar, and as of this morning *the prompts that built the page* are public. The footnote should simply hand all of that over. My recommendation:

> \* The receipts: every demo below answers when you press it, its source sits one click down inside each panel, and even the prompts that built this page are public. Press something before you believe any of it.

The three-item inventory is the §3 texture move (literal receipts, not rhetoric), the checkpoints claim is the one no other landing page can make, and the closing imperative honors the skeptic without flattering them — while feeding the CTA's verb-world ("Start poking"). It also stays clear of the neighboring "Nothing on this page is a mockup. We checked twice." — receipts here, wink there, no doubled move.

A quieter alternative if you want the footnote pointing at *immediate* evidence instead of the page-wide claim:

> \* Proof over promise: the readout below was minted by the server — the first line baked before you arrived, the second streamed in just for you. Everything past it answers the same way, source included.

I prefer the first — it's the fuller hand-over, and "press something before you believe any of it" is the sentence this page has been trying to say since the hero was written. If you take either, the GIF line's rejection is also a §6-worthy evidence row (no existing rule names the manufactured-shared-experience failure — it's now bitten us twice). Your pick?

content.thinking:
This is a new feature request for sticky Contents navigation, and his phrasing feels proposal-flavored, inviting my take rather than a direct build order. Given there are real design decisions here—what the sticky bar looks like, where it sits, mobile behavior—I should lay out a short design with options and a recommendation before building, rather than assuming a quick "go."

Looking at the current structure, the Contents section lives inside the hero container with its chapter grid, so simply making it sticky won't work since position:sticky is bound to its parent and would stop once the hero ends. I'm weighing two approaches: sticking the existing full Contents row (which has issues with height and mobile layout), versus introducing a slimmer mini-nav bar that fades in once the original Contents scrolls out of view—the latter seems like the more standard, practical pattern.

I'm now thinking through how to make a nav element stick for the rest of the page rather than just within the hero, considering whether it needs to be restructured as a sibling of the hero, and whether overflow properties like overflow-x: clip on ancestor elements might interfere with sticky positioning behavior.

I'm weighing whether to extract Contents into a page-level sticky bar, but worry a tall block eating viewport space when stuck. Maybe a compact sticky strip separate from the roomy hero Contents is cleaner — keep the hero grid as-is and add a slim "01 02 03 04 05" bar that appears once scrolled past.

But that risks duplicating the nav, which clashes with the minimalist approach. I'm leaning toward restyling the existing Contents element itself to be inherently slim enough to stick comfortably, since at larger screens it's already close to a single row — dropping the separate heading could make it compact enough to work as both the hero block and the sticky bar.

On mobile, five items won't fit one row, so I'm thinking a horizontal scrollable row without wrapping is the standard pattern to handle that. For the sticky styling, I'm planning a translucent blurred background with a bottom border when stuck, sitting below other layers since the navbar itself isn't sticky.

Scroll-margin on sections already accounts for the sticky bar's offset, so anchor links should land correctly. I'm deciding to skip scroll-spy active highlighting for v1 since it'd require client JS in an otherwise zero-JS nav — anchors alone should suffice, though I'll note it as a future enhancement. I'm also weighing whether the sticky bar, as a sibling above main, would persist through later sections like roadmap and FAQ, which might be mildly noisy but acceptable for v1.

I've found a cleaner solution: wrapping the sticky bar and the demo sections together in their own parent div so the sticky behavior naturally releases once that wrapper ends after the last demo, rather than sticking all the way to the footer. This means restructuring page.tsx so the hero no longer owns the contents/nav section — instead I'll extract it into a new zero-JS server component, ContentsNav, placed right after the hero in the page layout.

I'm also checking the mobile footnote placement, confirming the sticky bar's z-index and backdrop blur won't conflict with hover-card portals or reveal animations, and settling on a translucent blurred background style for the bar. The plan feels solid enough to move forward with implementation.

content.text:
Good instinct — five exhibits deep, the trip back up is real friction. Before building: the design has three decisions worth agreeing on, and one structural subtlety.

**The subtlety first:** `position: sticky` pins only within its parent, and the Contents currently lives *inside* the hero — it would stick for zero pixels. It has to move out to page level. That constraint actually produces the cleanest design: the Contents section leaves `hero.tsx` and becomes its own component rendered immediately after the hero — visually the same spot — wrapped in a parent that **ends after demo 05**, so the bar pins while you're among the exhibits and naturally scrolls away once you pass the last one. No nav noise over the roadmap, cohort, and FAQ, and sticky-release does it for free. (Happy accident: the page root already uses `overflow-x-clip` rather than `hidden` — chosen for the scroll reveals — which is exactly what keeps viewport-sticky working.)

**The three decisions, with my calls:**

1. **One element, not two.** No duplicate mini-nav appearing on scroll — the existing Contents itself becomes the sticky bar, slimmed to a single row: `contents · 01 the boundary · 02 the shell · …` in the mono register, "Contents" folded from a heading into a leading label. Zero JavaScript — no IntersectionObserver, no appear-on-scroll choreography. It's simply there, then pinned.
2. **Mobile: horizontal scroll, not wrap.** Five items can't fit a phone row; a wrapped sticky grid eats a third of the viewport. One `overflow-x-auto` row keeps the pinned cost to ~44px everywhere.
3. **Stuck styling is the only styling:** `bg-background/90` + backdrop blur + hairline bottom border from the start, so there's no visual mode-switch to engineer. Anchor offsets already work — sections carry `scroll-mt-16`, comfortably clearing the bar.

Explicitly deferred: active-section highlighting (scroll-spy). It needs client JS on an otherwise zero-JS nav, and the demos' own gauges already tell you where you are; can be added later if the plain version feels insufficient.

Touches: `hero.tsx` (contents section moves out), new `components/contents-nav.tsx`, `page.tsx` (sticky wrapper around the five exhibits). Green light?

Eric wants me to apply Brian Greene's walkthrough register — concrete scene first, abstract terms introduced only after their referent exists, explicit cues telling the reader where to look — to the intros of the other demos. He wants a before/after comparison for review, no actual edits yet, so I'm working through demos 01, 03, 04, and 05 against that register.

Looking at demo 01's boundary intro, the first paragraph already does this well: the "purchase" framing is concrete, with specific things bought and paid for (useState, database calls, API keys). The second paragraph contrasts two cards — one rendered server-side, one hydrated client-side — which sets up a clear scene for the reader to follow.

I'm testing a revision that grounds "hydration" concretely before naming it: showing the card "waking up" in the tab, then labeling that waking as hydration, while keeping the well-liked closing line about knowing the Node version. But the phrasing linking hydration to why the button waits feels slightly off — hydration isn't really the cause of the click-waiting, so I need to untangle that connection.

Now I'm moving to the streaming demo, drafting two paragraphs: one explaining that the static shell ships immediately while slow parts stream in as they finish, and another noting the delays are hardcoded but the streaming itself is genuine — each row is a real Server Component finishing on the server, not a faked animation.

I'm flagging that P1 leans on too many unexplained terms — "static shell," "fallback," "same response" — before the reader has a concrete referent. I want to rewrite it using the exhibit's own metaphor rather than importing a new one, and I'm realizing the natural fit is a kitchen/restaurant scene: the kitchen sends each dish out as soon as it's ready instead of holding the whole order, which extends the bakery/kitchen world already established elsewhere in the exhibit.

But I'm second-guessing that choice since it sits right next to a bakery-themed exhibit, which risks reusing the same construction twice in a row — so I'm weighing alternatives like a shipping/delivery scene before deciding to just stick with the demo's own concrete elements: the three rows, the skeletons, the delays, the single response.

I'm drafting the actual copy now, trying to describe the streaming behavior without leaning on a heavy metaphor — something like the page shipping instantly while slow parts leave placeholder "bones" that fill in as they finish, all within the same response. I want to keep "static shell" as the term since it's already introduced earlier in the reading order, so I'm aiming for cross-exhibit consistency rather than inventing new vocabulary.

P2 already has the escort phrase, so I'll leave it as is. Moving to demo 04 on mutation: P1 explains that a Server Action lives on the server and plugs directly into a form's action, skipping the need for an endpoint, fetch call, or JSON contract — the form calls the function, which mutates state and lets Next.js re-render around the result. P2 describes a counter held in an httpOnly cookie, read back by a Server Component, with the client-side JavaScript unable to touch that value even if it tried.

Reviewing this: P1 is decent but "mutates" feels too abstract and jargon-y compared to the concrete demo action of simply adding one to a number, and it's missing an escort line. P2 drops "httpOnly cookie" without grounding it, so I want to add a clarifying phrase explaining that httpOnly means the browser carries the cookie but JavaScript can't read it. I'm revising P1 to keep the endpoint/fetch/JSON contrast, then add an escort inviting the reader to press the button and follow the trip as the form calls the function, adds one, and the page updates.

For P2, I'm settling on a version that explains the cookie is httpOnly, defines what that means inline, notes a Server Component reads it back, and keeps the strong closing line about the browser's JavaScript never touching that value.

Moving to the image demo: P1 explains that ImageResponse renders JSX into a PNG at request time, functioning as a route handler — query in, image out — so one file generates the card for every page. P2 grounds it concretely: type a title and the server draws it, and the same endpoint generated this page's own link preview, inviting the reader to paste the URL into Slack to verify. I'm judging this draft as solid already, with "query in, image out" being nicely concrete and P2 doing good work to anchor the abstraction in something checkable, though I note JSX might need framing for non-developer readers.

I'm checking the other panels for factual accuracy too — the skeleton placeholders and httpOnly cookie behavior both check out. But I notice my P2 draft risks duplicating language already in the panel itself, since the existing copy already says JavaScript "never touches" the cookie value while the panel separately says it "can't even see it" — adding my own httpOnly explanation would pile a third overlapping phrase onto that same point, so I should ground it more briefly instead.

I'll keep the current ending as-is since it shipped alongside the panel copy and is tolerated, just inserting a short grounding clause before it. For the final write-up, I'll format each demo as terse Before/After blocks with a one-line rationale tied to the Greene tell, note that no edits are applied yet, and explicitly call out which sections I deliberately left untouched.

Draft pass done — worked against the §1 Greene entry (concrete scene first, abstract word only after its referent exists, the reader told where to look) and its tell (two unintroduced terms meeting in one clause). Restraint applied: demo 01's purchase paragraph, demo 03's confession paragraph, and demo 05's Slack paragraph are already doing Greene's job and stay untouched. Nothing edited yet — the proposals:

---

**Demo 01 — P2** *(the tell: "hydrated" arrives as unintroduced jargon; no escort)*

> **Before:** One of these cards rendered in Node.js and arrived as finished HTML. The other hydrated in your tab and is waiting for a click. Only one of them knows what version of Node it is running on.

> **After:** Watch the two cards below. One rendered in Node.js and arrived as finished HTML — done before you got here. The other arrived as JavaScript and woke up in your tab — the waking is called hydration — and its button is waiting for a click. Only one of them knows what version of Node it is running on.

The concrete image (*woke up in your tab*) comes first, the term is named after, and the closing line — the paragraph's best — is untouched.

---

**Demo 03 — P1** *(the tell: "fallback" and "streams into place over the same response" meet before either has a referent)*

> **Before:** Not any more. The static shell ships immediately, each slow part shows its fallback, and the server streams finished HTML into place over the same response as each part finishes. Nothing waits for everything.

> **After:** Not any more. The static shell ships immediately, and each slow part leaves behind a fallback — the gray placeholder you'll watch below. As each part finishes, the server streams its finished HTML down the same response, and the placeholder gives way. Nothing waits for everything.

"Fallback" gets pointed at the actual gray skeletons; the stream becomes a sequence you follow rather than a clause you parse. ("Static shell" stays unexplained on purpose — exhibit 02 teaches it one section earlier; the order is the curriculum.)

---

**Demo 04 — P1 and P2** *(P1: "the function mutates" is the abstract verb where the demo's concrete act is adding one; P2: "httpOnly cookie" and "read back by a Server Component" is the tell verbatim)*

> **Before (P1):** …The form calls the function, the function mutates, and Next.js re-renders the page around the result.

> **After (P1):** …Press the button below and follow the trip: the form calls the function, the function adds one, and Next.js re-renders the page around the new number.

> **Before (P2):** This one increments a counter held in an httpOnly cookie, read back by a Server Component. The JavaScript in your tab never touches that value, and could not if it tried.

> **After (P2):** This one keeps its count in a cookie your browser carries but your JavaScript cannot open — that is what httpOnly means — and a Server Component reads it back. The JavaScript in your tab never touches the value, and could not if it tried.

---

**Demo 05 — P1, one clause** *(light touch: "JSX" and "at request time" grounded for the aspirant without slowing the senior)*

> **Before:** You'll design one. ImageResponse renders JSX to a PNG at request time, and it is a route handler like any other — query in, image out. …

> **After:** You'll design one. ImageResponse turns JSX — the same markup your components are made of — into a PNG the moment a request asks, and it is a route handler like any other: query in, image out. …

---

All claims stay panel-true (the waking is real hydration, the gray placeholders render every run since the delays are hardcoded, the cookie is genuinely unreadable from the tab), and none of the drafts pre-spend a panel caption. Approve all four, or mark the ones to take?
